title: The Promise of the Whole Tree
story:
Then Krishna asked her to name the thing itself. Sitting close to his queen, who still would not lift her eyes from the ground, he said that her sorrow seemed to burn through all his limbs. What was the cause of her grief? If there was no harm in it, if it was proper for an affectionate husband to hear it, he entreated her on his life to reveal it to him.

And Satyabhama, seated with her countenance cast down toward the earth, spoke in a voice choked with the vapour of grief. "It was your own self that established my honor and my prosperity in days gone by," she said, "and that honor and that prosperity have become famous in the world. That I was most beloved of thee among all thy wives — that is what prompted me to raise my head with pride above all others. But my maids have told me, as they have heard it said, that today I have been laughed at by my co-wives and by other people. I hear that the Parijata flower that Narada gave thee, thou hast given to thy dear one, totally neglecting my poor self. By presenting her with that best of precious things thou hast given unmistakable expression to thy regard for her. Narada eulogized her in thy presence, and thou surely wert gratified hearing that praise of thy dear wife. But even if the sage had his reasons for praising her, why was the name of this unfortunate one uttered in that connection?

"If I am to repent for having tasted the sweet liquor of thy love," she went on, her voice rising, "it is better I should have nothing to do with it. Be kindly pleased to accord me thy permission. I could not have believed even in a dream that thou wouldst honor somebody else more than myself — but alas, it has come to pass in real life, even before the eyes of others. Perhaps the sage Narada has conceived a love for her; my grief is that thou wert present in the scene. Thou hast told me that people live for honor only. So, thus dishonored, I do not desire to live any longer. My source of protection has turned today into my source of fear.

"Renounced by thee, I shall be reduced to the condition of the white lily. How could I, who was thy beloved wife and am now discarded, look upon these Raivataka hills decked with the flowers of spring? How could I breathe this pure breeze, ringing with the notes of the cuckoo and fraught with the fragrance of flowers? How could I, who once sported on thy lap inside the waters of this ocean, glance at it again in my unhappy condition? Thou didst tell me in days gone by: 'O daughter of Satrajit, know that there is no wife of mine dearer to me than thyself.' What of that assurance now? Who cares to remember it?" Her voice broke into a kind of bitter laughter. "I did not know thee before to be so much of a cheat and a knave, but now I have come to know thee as fickle, deceiving, and partial to my rival. I have read thy secret thoughts by thy articulations and thy features, O thief, although thou triest to conceal them. Thy tongue only is honeyed, but thou art too guileful."

When the resentful daughter of Satrajit had spoken, Krishna consoled her. "Say not so, O lotus-eyed one, dearest ruler of my heart. What shall I tell thee more, my darling? Know me to be thine entirely. To please me, the sage Narada of unimpeachable deeds gave that flower to her out of generous feeling or regard for her — but I did not give it with my own hands."

Then he made the vow that changed everything. "What to speak of a single flower — I shall fetch that best of all trees, the Parijata tree itself, from the gardens of paradise, and keep it in thy mansion. So be it, then; this shall be my foremost concern."

The storm in Satyabhama's eyes faltered. She had asked, in her grief, to be remembered; he had answered by promising her a tree from heaven — not the flower that had wounded her, but the whole tree it had come from, uprooted and planted in her own courtyard. Whatever she had expected from her accusation, it was not this.
reflection: Satyabhama's long accusation is a precise anatomy of a wounded pride, and its sharpest lines are those of a woman testing whether she is still loved. Krishna's answer is not to argue with any of it but to outbid the wound: against one flower he sets a whole tree of paradise, as if the only way to prove where his heart lives is to give more than the rival received.
next_story_tease: But the tree belonged to Indra's heaven, and to bring it down Krishna would have to ask a king of gods who had no wish to part with it.
hero_scene: Satyabhama seated with her face cast down and her palm against her cheek, tears on her lashes, while Krishna leans close with his hand raised in a vow, his expression tender and resolute, the promise of the whole Parijata tree hanging between them in the lamplight.

Krishna leaning close, hand raised in a vow
the lamplit apartment in Satyabhama's mansion
the faded white garment she wears
the imagined Parijata tree glowing faintly beyond the window
